title: Socrates and Crito: The Inviolability of Moral Principle and Law — 399 BCE
summary: In 399 BCE Athens, when his wealthy friend Crito bribed the guards to arrange his escape from execution, Socrates refused to flee, arguing that one must never answer injustice with lawlessness.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 156: அண்ணாவின் அரிசி வாக்குறுதி: “மூன்று படி இலக்கு; ஒரு படி நிச்சயம்”
full_text:
In the dim pre-dawn hours of 399 BCE, inside a stone prison in Athens, the seventy-year-old philosopher Socrates lay peacefully asleep awaiting execution by hemlock.

The heavy wooden door creaked open. His wealthy, devoted friend Crito slipped into the cell, having successfully bribed the prison guards. Shaking Socrates awake, Crito urged him to hurry:
"Socrates, awaken! Everything is prepared. The guards are bought, a fast boat is waiting at Piraeus, and our friends in Thessaly will welcome you into exile. If you remain here and die, people will brand me as a cowardly friend who loved his gold more than your life! Besides, this Athenian court gave you an unjust verdict—why obey an injustice?"

Socrates sat up, serene and undisturbed, and asked Crito to sit beside him on the stone bench:
"My dear Crito, why should we care about the unexamined opinions of the multitude? Ought we not to listen only to reason and moral truth?

Consider the laws of Athens. These laws protected my parents' marriage, nurtured my childhood, and provided the civic order that permitted me to philosophize freely for seventy years. Now, flawed men have rendered an unjust verdict against me. If I break out of prison and flee, do I not assault the very concept of the rule of law itself?
Can one ever cure an injustice by committing another wrong? No! One must never return evil for evil, nor answer lawlessness with rebellion. If I flee now to save a few frail years of old age, I will destroy the integrity of every philosophical argument I ever uttered. It is far better to suffer an injustice than to commit one!"

Speechless with sorrow and awe, Crito bowed his head: "I have nothing to say, Socrates." Socrates chose death over dishonor, giving humanity its foundational lesson in civil integrity.
